title: Psychiatry & Behavioral Medicine
summary: How to interview a person in distress, recognize the major psychiatric diagnoses by their real criteria, spot the medical illnesses that imitate them, and act safely when someone is suicidal, agitated, or withdrawing. Built for the depth a PA program expects on day one.

lessons.title: The interview and the mental status exam
lessons.body:
Psychiatry has no blood test for most of what it treats. The exam *is* the conversation. That means the quality of your data depends on whether the person in front of you decides to tell you the truth, which depends on the first ninety seconds.

## Building the alliance

Sit down. Sit at eye level, closer to the door than the patient if safety is a question, and put the computer where it does not sit between your faces. Open with something that is not a symptom: what brought you in today, in your own words. Then shut up. The single most common interview error is interrupting, and clinicians interrupt on average within about `11` to `20` seconds of the patient starting.

Use the **open-to-closed funnel**. Start wide ("tell me what the last few weeks have been like"), narrow as you go ("how many hours are you actually sleeping?"), and finish with the yes/no screening questions you must ask ("have you had thoughts of killing yourself?"). Wide questions get you the story; narrow questions get you the criteria.

> **Key:** History is what the patient tells you. The mental status exam (MSE) is what you observe right now, in the room. Keep them separate in your head and in your note.

## The MSE, component by component

- **Appearance** — grooming, hygiene, dress appropriate to weather, apparent versus stated age, track marks, self-inflicted wounds.
- **Behavior and attitude** — eye contact, psychomotor slowing or agitation, cooperative, guarded, hostile.
- **Speech** — rate, rhythm, volume. Pressured speech (fast, hard to interrupt) points to mania; slow and quiet points to depression.
- **Mood versus affect** — mood is what the patient *says* they feel, in quotation marks: "I feel like a stone." Affect is what you *see*: euthymic, depressed, anxious, irritable, described by range (full, constricted, flat) and congruence with the stated mood.
- **Thought process** — the *form*: linear and goal-directed, circumstantial (wanders but arrives), tangential (wanders and never arrives), flight of ideas, loose associations, word salad.
- **Thought content** — the *what*: delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, intent.
- **Perception** — hallucinations, by sense. Auditory is the most common in primary psychiatric illness; new visual or tactile hallucinations should push you toward a medical or substance cause.
- **Cognition** — alert and oriented to person, place, time, situation; attention, memory.
- **Insight** — does the person believe they are ill?
- **Judgment** — are the decisions they describe making safe ones?

> **Trap:** "Mood: depressed, affect: depressed" tells the next clinician nothing. Quote the mood. Describe the affect.

## Cognitive screens and collateral

The Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores out of `30`; below `24` suggests impairment. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) also scores out of `30` with `26` and above considered normal, and it is more sensitive to mild impairment and executive dysfunction. Both are screens, not diagnoses.

Get **collateral**: family, the group home, the pharmacy, the old chart. A person in a manic or psychotic episode is often the least reliable narrator of their own last two weeks, and you are allowed to *receive* information from family even when confidentiality stops you from giving any out.

> **On shift:** Document the patient's own words in quotation marks. "I'm not going to make it to Friday" is evidence. "Patient appears depressed" is opinion.
keyPoints: History is reported; the MSE is observed right now — never blur them.
Mood is the patient's quoted words; affect is what you observe, with range and congruence.
Thought process is the form of thinking; thought content is the subject matter.
MMSE below 24 of 30, or MoCA below 26 of 30, is a screening flag, not a diagnosis.
Collateral history is standard of care in psychiatry, and you may receive it even when you cannot disclose.

checks.q: A patient says "I feel fine, honestly" while sitting motionless, tearful, and barely speaking above a whisper. How is this best documented?
choices: Mood: "I feel fine, honestly"; affect: depressed, constricted, incongruent with stated mood
Mood and affect both within normal limits per patient report
Affect: "I feel fine, honestly"; mood: tearful
checks.why: Mood is the patient's own quoted report; affect is your observation. When they disagree, say so — incongruence is a finding, not an error.

checks.q: A patient answers every question with a long detour through unrelated stories but eventually reaches the point. This thought process is:
checks.why: Circumstantial thinking wanders but arrives. Tangential wanders and never arrives. Loose associations and flight of ideas are more severe breaks in connection between thoughts.

checks.q: Which MSE finding most strongly suggests a medical or substance cause rather than a primary psychiatric illness?
choices: Auditory hallucinations of two voices commenting on the patient
Constricted affect with poor eye contact
checks.why: Auditory hallucinations are the most common type in primary psychiatric illness. New visual or tactile hallucinations point toward delirium, intoxication, or withdrawal until proven otherwise.

lessons.title: Mood disorders: depression and the bipolar spectrum
lessons.body:
Mood disorders are disorders of the *baseline*, not of the moment. Everyone has bad days. What makes a mood episode is a sustained shift that lasts a defined length of time and breaks function.

## Major depressive disorder

Major depressive disorder (MDD) needs **five of nine** symptoms present nearly every day for **at least two weeks**, and at least one of the five must be depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure (anhedonia). The classic memory hook is **SIGECAPS**, which lists the eight symptoms besides depressed mood:

- **S**leep — too much or too little; early-morning waking is characteristic
- **I**nterest — anhedonia
- **G**uilt — or worthlessness, often out of proportion
- **E**nergy — fatigue
- **C**oncentration — indecisiveness
- **A**ppetite — up or down, with weight change
- **P**sychomotor — agitation or retardation, and it must be observable by others
- **S**uicidality — recurrent thoughts of death, ideation, plan, or attempt

The symptoms must cause distress or impairment and must not be better explained by a substance or another medical condition. **Persistent depressive disorder** (dysthymia) is a lower-grade depressed mood present more days than not for **two years** in adults (one year in children and adolescents).

The **PHQ-9** scores the nine criteria from `0` to `3` each, so `0` to `27` total. Bands: `0-4` minimal, `5-9` mild, `10-14` moderate, `15-19` moderately severe, `20-27` severe. Item 9 asks directly about thoughts of being better off dead — any non-zero answer gets a live risk assessment, not a follow-up appointment.

> **Key:** Two weeks, five of nine, and one of the five must be depressed mood or anhedonia. That sentence is the whole diagnosis.

## Mania and hypomania

A **manic** episode is abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood *plus* increased energy or activity, lasting **at least 7 days** (or any duration if hospitalization is required), with three or more associated symptoms — four if the mood is only irritable. The associated symptoms are grandiosity, decreased need for sleep (feels rested on `3` hours, which is different from insomnia), pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and risky pleasurable activity. Mania causes marked impairment, or psychosis, or requires hospitalization.

**Hypomania** is the same symptom list lasting **at least 4 consecutive days**, clearly observable by others, but *not* severe enough to cause marked impairment or hospitalization, and with **no psychotic features** — if there is psychosis, it is mania by definition.

- **Bipolar I** requires one lifetime manic episode. Depression is common but not required.
- **Bipolar II** requires at least one hypomanic episode *and* at least one major depressive episode, and no manic episode ever.

Specifiers matter: **with mixed features** (depressive and manic symptoms together, a high-risk state for suicide), **with seasonal pattern**, and **with peripartum onset** (onset in pregnancy or within `4` weeks of delivery).

> **Trap:** Giving an antidepressant alone to someone with bipolar disorder can flip them into mania or accelerate cycling. Anyone presenting with depression gets screened for a past manic or hypomanic episode *before* an antidepressant is started.

> **On the exam:** "Slept 2 hours a night for a week, started three businesses, spent the rent" is mania. "Slept 2 hours a night and feels wrecked" is depression with insomnia. Decreased *need* for sleep is the discriminator.
keyPoints: MDD: 5 of 9 symptoms, 2 weeks, at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia.
PHQ-9 runs 0-27; 10-14 moderate, 20-27 severe; item 9 triggers a live risk assessment.
Mania is 7 days or any duration needing hospitalization; hypomania is 4 days with no psychosis and no marked impairment.
Bipolar I needs a manic episode; bipolar II needs hypomania plus a major depressive episode.
Screen every depressed patient for past mania before starting an antidepressant.

checks.q: A 24-year-old has had 5 days of elevated mood, sleeping 3 hours and feeling rested, talking rapidly, and spending heavily. She kept working and there is no psychosis. Most likely:
choices: Major depressive disorder with mixed features
checks.why: Four or more days, observable, but no marked impairment, no hospitalization, and no psychosis is hypomania. Mania requires 7 days or hospitalization-level severity.

checks.q: A patient scores 22 on the PHQ-9. This band is:
checks.why: PHQ-9 bands are 0-4 minimal, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, 20-27 severe.

lessons.title: Anxiety, trauma, and obsessive-compulsive disorders
lessons.body:
Anxiety is a normal alarm system. It becomes a disorder when the alarm fires without a fire, fires too long, or costs more than the danger it is protecting against. The diagnoses in this group are separated mostly by **what** the fear is about and **how long** it has lasted.

## The anxiety disorders

**Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)** is excessive worry about multiple domains, hard to control, on more days than not for **at least 6 months**, with three or more of: restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. In children, only one of the six is required.

A **panic attack** is a discrete surge of intense fear peaking within **10 minutes**, with four or more of thirteen symptoms — palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills or heat, numbness, derealization, fear of losing control, fear of dying. A panic attack is a modifier, not a diagnosis; it happens in many conditions. **Panic disorder** is recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus **1 month or more** of worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behavior to avoid them.

**Agoraphobia** is fear of two or more of: public transit, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds or lines, being outside the home alone — `6` months or more. **Social anxiety disorder** is fear of scrutiny in social or performance situations, `6` months or more. **Specific phobia** is a circumscribed fear (heights, needles, dogs), also `6` months or more.

The **GAD-7** scores `0` to `21`: `5` mild, `10` moderate, `15` severe. `10` or higher is the usual referral threshold.

> **Trap:** First panic attack after age `45`, or with focal neurologic signs, syncope, or abnormal vitals, is a medical workup — think arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma — not a psychiatric diagnosis.

## Trauma- and stressor-related

**PTSD** requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence — directly, as a witness, by learning it happened to a close other, or through repeated extreme occupational exposure. Then four symptom clusters:

1. **Intrusion** — nightmares, flashbacks, intrusive memories
2. **Avoidance** — of reminders, thoughts, places, people
3. **Negative changes in cognition and mood** — numbing, blame, amnesia for part of the event
4. **Arousal and reactivity** — hypervigilance, startle, irritability, poor sleep, reckless behavior

Duration must be **more than 1 month**. The same picture lasting **3 days to 1 month** is **acute stress disorder**. **Adjustment disorder** is distress out of proportion to an identifiable non-traumatic stressor, beginning within `3` months and resolving within `6` months of the stressor ending.

> **Key:** The 1-month line is the whole trick. Under a month with a qualifying trauma is acute stress disorder; over a month is PTSD.

## Obsessive-compulsive and related

**Obsessions** are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that raise anxiety. **Compulsions** are repetitive behaviors or mental acts done to reduce that anxiety, often following rigid rules. The loop is the disorder: the compulsion works for minutes and strengthens the obsession for good. To qualify, the symptoms take more than `1` hour a day or cause marked distress or impairment. Insight is usually preserved — people with OCD generally know the thoughts are irrational, which separates OCD from a delusion.

Also in this family, at recognition level: **body dysmorphic disorder** (preoccupation with a perceived flaw others barely notice, with repetitive mirror-checking) and **hoarding disorder** (persistent difficulty discarding possessions, with living areas so cluttered they cannot be used for their purpose).

> **On shift:** Someone in a full panic attack is not being dramatic. Coach slow breathing, reduce stimulation, stay with them, and check a glucose, a rhythm, and an oxygen saturation before you call it psychiatric.
keyPoints: GAD, social anxiety, specific phobia, and agoraphobia all carry a 6-month duration requirement.
Panic attacks peak within 10 minutes; panic disorder adds 1 month of anticipatory worry or avoidance.
GAD-7 runs 0-21 with cutoffs at 5, 10, and 15; 10 or higher usually prompts referral.
PTSD requires more than 1 month; 3 days to 1 month with the same picture is acute stress disorder.
OCD obsessions raise anxiety, compulsions lower it briefly, and insight is usually intact.

checks.q: Three weeks after surviving a car crash, a patient has nightmares, avoids driving, is hypervigilant, and startles easily. The diagnosis is:
checks.why: Three weeks is inside the 3-day to 1-month window, so this is acute stress disorder. PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month. GAD requires 6 months of multi-domain worry.

checks.q: A 52-year-old man has his first ever episode of crushing chest pressure, sweating, and a sense of doom. The most appropriate next step is:
choices: Diagnose panic disorder and start an SSRI
Reassure and discharge with breathing exercises
Work up medical causes including ACS, arrhythmia, and PE
checks.why: A first panic-like episode after age 45 is a medical workup until proven otherwise. Panic disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion at that age, and it also requires recurrent attacks.

checks.q: Which best distinguishes an obsession in OCD from a delusion in psychosis?
choices: The person with OCD usually recognizes the thought as irrational
checks.why: Insight is usually preserved in OCD — the thought is experienced as unwanted and senseless. A delusion is held as true despite contrary evidence.

lessons.title: Psychosis and the schizophrenia spectrum
lessons.body:
Psychosis is a break in the ability to tell what is real. It is a *symptom*, like chest pain, and it has a long list of causes. Schizophrenia is only one of them, and it is not the most common cause of a first episode in an emergency department.

## Positive versus negative symptoms

**Positive symptoms** are things added to normal experience: hallucinations (most often auditory), delusions (fixed false beliefs — persecutory, grandiose, referential, somatic), disorganized speech, and disorganized or catatonic behavior. They respond reasonably well to antipsychotics because they track excess dopamine signaling in the mesolimbic pathway.

**Negative symptoms** are things subtracted: flat affect, poverty of speech (alogia), loss of motivation (avolition), loss of pleasure (anhedonia), social withdrawal. They respond poorly to medication and they drive long-term disability more than the hallucinations do. **Cognitive symptoms** — working memory, attention, executive function — sit alongside them.

> **Key:** Positive symptoms get people admitted. Negative and cognitive symptoms determine whether they ever work again.

## Sorting the spectrum by the clock

- **Brief psychotic disorder** — `1` day to **less than 1 month**, with full return to baseline.
- **Schizophreniform disorder** — **1 to 6 months** of the schizophrenia symptom picture.
- **Schizophrenia** — **6 months or more** of continuous disturbance, including at least `1` month of active-phase symptoms (two or more of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms — and at least one must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech).
- **Schizoaffective disorder** — a mood episode plus psychosis, *and* at least `2` weeks of delusions or hallucinations with **no** prominent mood episode. That two-week window is what separates it from a mood disorder with psychotic features.
- **Delusional disorder** — `1` month or more of delusions with otherwise normal functioning and no other active-phase symptoms. These people often look fine until you touch the belief.

## The first-break workup

A first episode of psychosis is a medical evaluation. Reasonable elements: vital signs including temperature, fingerstick glucose, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, TSH, urine drug screen, urinalysis (especially in older adults), pregnancy test where applicable, and neuroimaging when the presentation is atypical — new focal findings, first episode after age `40`, headache, seizure, rapid cognitive decline. Add HIV, RPR, and vitamin B12 when history supports it.

Causes that are not primary psychiatric illness: stimulant intoxication, cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids, alcohol withdrawal, steroids, anticholinergics, delirium from infection, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, thyroid disease, autoimmune encephalitis, temporal lobe epilepsy, brain tumor, Huntington disease, Wilson disease, and neurosyphilis.

> **Trap:** Age of onset is a clue, not a rule. Schizophrenia typically appears in the late teens to mid-20s in men and the late 20s to early 30s in women. A brand-new psychosis in a `68`-year-old is far more likely to be delirium, dementia, or a medication than schizophrenia.

## Prognosis and course

Better outcomes track with: later onset, acute onset, an obvious precipitant, prominent mood symptoms, good premorbid function, being female, and a short duration of untreated psychosis. Worse outcomes track with: early insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, poor premorbid function, family history, and substance use. Lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia is roughly `0.3%` to `0.7%`. Suicide risk is substantial — roughly `5%` die by suicide — which is why the negative and depressive symptoms are not a footnote.

> **On shift:** Do not argue with a delusion and do not agree with it. "I don't hear the voices, but I believe that you do, and I can see it's frightening" keeps you in the room.
keyPoints: Positive symptoms are added experiences; negative symptoms are subtracted capacities and drive disability.
Brief psychotic disorder is under 1 month, schizophreniform 1-6 months, schizophrenia 6 months or more.
Schizoaffective requires 2 or more weeks of psychosis without a prominent mood episode.
A first psychotic episode gets glucose, vitals, labs, urine drug screen, and imaging when atypical.
New psychosis over age 40, or with visual hallucinations, is medical until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A 21-year-old has had 10 weeks of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and disorganized speech, with no substance use and normal labs. The best current diagnosis is:
checks.why: Ten weeks falls in the 1-to-6-month band, which is schizophreniform disorder. Schizophrenia requires 6 months or more of continuous disturbance; brief psychotic disorder resolves in under a month.

checks.q: Which finding most argues against a primary psychiatric cause of new psychosis?
choices: Fever, disorientation, and visual hallucinations in a 70-year-old
checks.why: Fever, disorientation, and visual hallucinations in an older adult describe delirium. Auditory hallucinations, delusions, and flat affect are all common in primary psychiatric illness.

lessons.title: Personality, eating, and neurodevelopmental conditions
lessons.body:
These three groups share one feature: they are patterns that show up early and persist, rather than episodes that come and go.

## Personality disorders: the three clusters

A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates from cultural expectation, is stable since adolescence or early adulthood, and causes impairment.

- **Cluster A, "odd"** — paranoid (pervasive distrust), schizoid (genuinely prefers solitude, no desire for relationships), schizotypal (odd beliefs, magical thinking, eccentric, social anxiety).
- **Cluster B, "dramatic"** — antisocial (disregard for others' rights, requires age `18` or older plus evidence of conduct disorder before age `15`), borderline (unstable relationships, identity, and affect, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, self-harm, chronic emptiness), histrionic (attention-seeking, shallow shifting emotion), narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, low empathy).
- **Cluster C, "anxious"** — avoidant (wants relationships but fears rejection — the contrast with schizoid), dependent (needs others to take responsibility), obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (rigid perfectionism and control, and unlike OCD, the traits feel correct to the person).

> **On shift:** With a person who has borderline personality disorder, splitting on the team is common. The fix is boundaries that are kind, explicit, and identical across every staff member, plus taking self-harm seriously every single time. Roughly `8%` to `10%` die by suicide.

## Eating disorders

**Anorexia nervosa** is restriction of intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbance in how body weight is experienced. Subtypes are restricting and binge-eating/purging. It is the deadliest psychiatric disorder by mortality rate, and the danger is medical: bradycardia below `40` beats per minute, hypotension, hypothermia, QT prolongation, low potassium, low magnesium, low phosphate, amenorrhea, osteopenia, and lanugo hair.

**Refeeding syndrome** is what kills people during treatment. When carbohydrate returns, insulin surges and drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells. Serum **phosphate** falls first and hardest, which can cause heart failure, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, and death. Refeed slowly, check electrolytes daily, and replace phosphate, potassium, and magnesium before and during.

**Bulimia nervosa** is recurrent binge eating with compensatory behavior (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise) at least once a week for `3` months, in someone usually of normal weight. Look for eroded dental enamel, parotid swelling, knuckle calluses (Russell sign), and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting.

**Binge-eating disorder** is bingeing without compensation, once a week for `3` months. **ARFID** (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder) is restriction driven by sensory aversion, lack of interest, or fear of choking — *without* body-image disturbance.

> **Trap:** Normal weight does not rule out a life-threatening eating disorder. Purging can drop potassium into arrhythmia range at any body mass index.

## Neurodevelopmental

**ADHD** requires `6` or more symptoms of inattention and/or `6` or more of hyperactivity-impulsivity (`5` if age `17` or older), present for at least `6` months, with several symptoms present **before age 12**, in **two or more settings**, causing impairment.

**Autism spectrum disorder** requires persistent deficits in social communication and interaction *plus* restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, present in early development. Severity is graded by support needs, levels `1` to `3`.

**Intellectual disability** requires deficits in intellectual function *and* in adaptive function, with onset in the developmental period. Modern criteria grade severity by adaptive function, not by IQ number alone.

> **Key:** Every diagnosis in this lesson is defined partly by *when it started*. Age of onset is the criterion students forget and exams test.
keyPoints: Cluster A odd, Cluster B dramatic, Cluster C anxious; avoidant wants closeness, schizoid does not.
Antisocial personality disorder requires age 18 or older plus conduct disorder before age 15.
Anorexia has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder; watch bradycardia and electrolytes.
Refeeding syndrome drops phosphate first — replace phosphate, potassium, and magnesium and refeed slowly.
ADHD needs symptoms before age 12, in two or more settings, for 6 months.

checks.q: A 19-year-old with anorexia nervosa is admitted at 68% of expected body weight and started on nutrition. On day 3 she develops weakness and confusion. The most likely electrolyte abnormality is:
checks.why: Refeeding syndrome drives phosphate intracellularly as insulin rises, producing hypophosphatemia with weakness, confusion, cardiac failure, and seizures. Potassium and magnesium also fall, not rise.

checks.q: A patient avoids social relationships because he is certain he will be humiliated, though he badly wants friends. This best fits:
checks.why: Avoidant personality disorder involves wanting relationships but fearing rejection. Schizoid patients genuinely do not desire relationships. Schizotypal adds odd beliefs and perceptual oddities.

lessons.title: Delirium, dementia, and the medical mimics
lessons.body:
The most dangerous mistake in behavioral health is calling a medical emergency a psychiatric one. Delirium is that emergency, and it wears a psychiatric mask more often than any other condition.

## Delirium versus dementia

**Delirium** is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over **hours to days**, **fluctuates** through the day, and is caused by something medical. The cardinal feature is **inattention** — the person cannot hold a train of thought, cannot recite the months backward, drifts mid-sentence. Consciousness level is altered. It is reversible when the cause is fixed, and it carries in-hospital mortality of roughly `20%` to `30%` when missed.

**Dementia** (major neurocognitive disorder) develops over **months to years**, is gradual and progressive, and attention and alertness stay intact until late. The two can coexist; dementia is the single biggest risk factor for delirium.

| Feature | Delirium | Dementia |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Hours to days | Months to years |
| Course | Fluctuates | Slowly progressive |
| Attention | Impaired, the core sign | Preserved until late |
| Alertness | Altered | Normal |
| Reversible | Often | Rarely |

Delirium comes in three motor subtypes: **hyperactive** (agitated, the one everyone notices), **hypoactive** (quiet, withdrawn, mistaken for depression — the most common and the most missed, with the worst outcomes), and mixed.

> **Key:** Acute change in mental status plus inattention equals delirium until proven otherwise. Look for the cause; do not sedate the question away.

## The workup

Vitals with temperature and oxygen saturation, fingerstick glucose, medication review (the highest-yield step in older adults), complete blood count, electrolytes with calcium, renal and liver function, urinalysis and culture, chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and a pulse oximetry check. Add head imaging for head trauma, focal findings, or anticoagulation; add lumbar puncture for fever with meningeal signs. **DIMS** is one workable frame: **D**rugs, **I**nfection, **M**etabolic, **S**tructural.

## The dementias, at recognition

- **Alzheimer disease** — most common. Gradual short-term memory loss first, then language and visuospatial decline. Amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
- **Vascular dementia** — stepwise decline with focal neurologic findings, in a patient with vascular risk factors.
- **Lewy body dementia** — fluctuating cognition, well-formed **visual hallucinations**, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics. Giving haloperidol here can be catastrophic.
- **Frontotemporal dementia** — earlier onset, typically `45` to `65`. Personality change, disinhibition, and loss of empathy come *before* memory loss, so it is often misread as a primary psychiatric illness.

## The medical mimics

Every one of these can present looking purely psychiatric:

- **Hypothyroidism** — depression, slowing, cold intolerance. **Hyperthyroidism** — anxiety, tremor, weight loss, palpitations.
- **Hypoglycemia** — anxiety, confusion, bizarre behavior, combativeness. Check a glucose on *everyone*.
- **Hypoxia and hypercapnia** — restlessness and confusion long before cyanosis.
- **Infection** — urinary tract infection, pneumonia, and sepsis in older adults often present as confusion with no fever.
- **Vitamin B12 deficiency** — dementia, psychosis, paresthesias, and a macrocytic anemia that may lag the neuro signs.
- **Wilson disease** — young person with psychiatric symptoms, tremor, liver disease, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
- **Huntington disease** — chorea, personality change, and a family history, onset typically `30` to `50`.
- **Neurosyphilis** — personality change, cognitive decline, and a positive RPR.
- **Brain lesions** — frontal tumors, subdural hematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus (the triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline).
- **Medications** — corticosteroids (mania or psychosis), anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, levetiracetam, interferon.

> **Trap:** The quiet, withdrawn older adult who "just seems depressed" after surgery is hypoactive delirium far more often than new-onset depression. Test attention before you accept a mood diagnosis.
keyPoints: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattention, medical cause, often reversible.
Hypoactive delirium is the most common subtype and is routinely mistaken for depression.
Dementia is gradual with preserved attention until late; the two often coexist.
Lewy body dementia brings visual hallucinations and dangerous antipsychotic sensitivity.
Check glucose, oxygen saturation, temperature, and the medication list on every acute mental status change.

checks.q: An 82-year-old is confused and drowsy today after two days of gradually worsening disorientation that is worse at night. Attention is impaired. The most likely diagnosis is:
checks.why: Acute onset over days, fluctuation with a nighttime worsening, and impaired attention define delirium. Dementia progresses over months to years with attention preserved until late.

checks.q: Which dementia is most associated with well-formed visual hallucinations and severe antipsychotic sensitivity?
checks.why: Lewy body dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and dangerous sensitivity to antipsychotics such as haloperidol.

checks.q: A 28-year-old has new psychosis, a tremor, and elevated liver enzymes. The mimic to consider is:
checks.why: Wilson disease is copper accumulation presenting in young adults with psychiatric symptoms, movement abnormality, liver disease, and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Huntington brings chorea and family history, typically later.

lessons.title: Suicide risk, violence, and keeping everyone safe
lessons.body:
Safety work is the part of psychiatry that is unforgiving. It is also the part that is mostly procedure, which means you can learn to do it well before you know much else.

## Assessing suicide risk

Ask directly. The single most durable myth in this field is that asking about suicide plants the idea; it does not, and the evidence is consistent. Ask plainly: "Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?" Then walk the ladder: **ideation** (passive — "I wish I wouldn't wake up" — versus active), **plan** (how specific?), **intent** (do they mean to act?), **means** (do they have access?), **rehearsal** or preparatory acts, and **past attempts**, which is the strongest single predictor.

Static risk factors: prior attempt, male sex (higher completion; women attempt more often), age over `65` or adolescence, psychiatric diagnosis, substance use, chronic pain or terminal illness, family history of suicide, recent loss, access to firearms, incarceration. Protective factors: children at home, pregnancy, strong social connection, religious objection to suicide, engagement in treatment, reasons for living the person can name. Protective factors reduce risk; they never zero it out.

Tools you should recognize: the **Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)**, a structured question set now standard in many emergency departments, and **SAD PERSONS**, an older mnemonic with poor predictive value that still appears on exams. Neither replaces judgment.

> **Key:** Means restriction is the highest-yield intervention in the whole conversation. Firearms out of the home, medications locked or reduced in quantity. Most suicidal crises are short.

## The safety plan

A safety plan is written *with* the patient, not handed to them: warning signs they recognize, internal coping steps, people and places that distract, people they can ask for help, professionals and crisis lines to call, and the means-restriction step. In the United States, `988` is the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Room safety in the emergency department: change the patient into a gown, search belongings and remove sharps, cords, belts, shoelaces, lighters, and medications, remove equipment and tubing from the room, use a room with clear line of sight, and assign continuous observation when risk is high. Document that you did it.

## Violence risk and the agitation ladder

The best predictor of future violence is past violence. Other flags: intoxication, psychosis with persecutory or command themes, agitation, pacing, clenched fists, loud speech, and invaded personal space.

Position yourself first: stay closer to the exit, keep more than an arm's length, remove your stethoscope and badge lanyard, and never enter alone if your instincts say not to.

Then climb the ladder in order:

1. **Verbal de-escalation** — one speaker, calm tone, short sentences, name the emotion, offer choices (food, blanket, phone call), set limits without threats. This resolves the majority of agitation episodes.
2. **Environmental** — quiet room, dim lights, fewer people, remove the trigger, bring a family member if they help.
3. **Chemical** — offer oral medication first because participation is therapeutic. Common regimens vary by protocol; a frequent combination is an antipsychotic with or without a benzodiazepine, and for suspected alcohol withdrawal or stimulant intoxication a benzodiazepine alone is often preferred.
4. **Physical restraint** — last resort, for imminent danger to self or others only, never for convenience or punishment.

## Restraint rules

Restraint requires a provider order, with federal time limits: `4` hours for adults `18` and older, `2` hours for ages `9` to `17`, and `1` hour for children under `9`, with re-evaluation to renew. Use enough trained staff — commonly `5` people, one per limb and one for the head. Never restrain prone or with anything across the chest or neck; positional asphyxia kills. Monitor circulation, airway, breathing, skin, and toileting on a set schedule, and remove restraints as soon as the criteria are gone.

> **On shift:** "I need you to sit down" is a demand. "I can get you something to eat, and I need you in this chair while I do it" is a choice plus a limit. The second one works far more often.
keyPoints: Asking directly about suicide does not create risk; plan, intent, and means define its severity.
A prior attempt is the strongest single predictor of a future one.
Means restriction plus a co-written safety plan is the highest-yield outpatient intervention.
Climb the agitation ladder: verbal, then environmental, then chemical, then physical restraint.
Restraint orders are time-limited — 4 hours adults, 2 hours ages 9-17, 1 hour under 9 — and never prone.

checks.q: A patient in the emergency department is pacing, shouting, and has not yet threatened anyone. The first intervention should be:
choices: Verbal de-escalation with a single calm speaker
Security escort out of the department
checks.why: Verbal de-escalation is the first rung and resolves most agitation. Chemical and physical restraint are reserved for imminent danger after less restrictive options fail.

checks.q: Which is the strongest single predictor of a future suicide attempt?
checks.why: Prior attempt is the strongest single predictor. The others raise risk but are far weaker predictors on their own.

lessons.title: Substance use disorders and withdrawal
lessons.body:
DSM-5 collapsed abuse and dependence into a single **substance use disorder** graded by how many of `11` criteria are met: `2-3` mild, `4-5` moderate, `6` or more severe. The criteria cluster into impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacologic features (tolerance, withdrawal). Tolerance and withdrawal alone in someone taking a prescribed medication as directed do not make a disorder.

## Alcohol

Screening: **CAGE** (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) — `2` or more positives is a flag. **AUDIT** is `10` items, `0-40`, with `8` or more suggesting hazardous use.

Withdrawal runs on a clock, and knowing the clock is the whole point:

| Time after last drink | What happens |
|---|---|
| `6-12` hours | Tremor, anxiety, sweating, nausea, tachycardia |
| `12-24` hours | Alcoholic hallucinosis — usually visual, with intact orientation |
| `24-48` hours | Withdrawal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic |
| `48-72` hours and beyond | Delirium tremens |

**Delirium tremens** is confusion plus autonomic storm — fever, tachycardia, hypertension, profound diaphoresis — and it carries mortality around `5%` treated, far higher untreated. It is a critical-care problem, not an observation problem.

Treatment is **benzodiazepines**, dosed to symptoms using the **CIWA-Ar** scale (`10` items, score `0-67`; treat at roughly `8-10` or more). Longer-acting agents such as diazepam or chlordiazepoxide are typical; lorazepam is preferred in liver disease because it is not oxidatively metabolized. Add thiamine `100` mg or more, folate, magnesium, and fluids.

> **Key:** Give **thiamine before glucose**. A glucose load in a thiamine-deficient person can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

**Wernicke encephalopathy** is the acute, reversible triad of confusion, ataxia, and eye findings (ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus) — often incomplete. **Korsakoff syndrome** is the chronic, largely irreversible sequel: anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

Maintenance options: naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram.

## Opioids

Overdose is the **triad**: depressed consciousness, respiratory depression, **pinpoint pupils**. Respiratory failure kills, not the sedation. **Naloxone** reverses it: `0.4` to `2` mg intravenously, intramuscularly, or intranasally (`4` mg intranasal is the common community device), repeated every `2-3` minutes as needed. Its half-life is shorter than most opioids, so re-sedation is expected — especially with methadone or fentanyl — and observation is mandatory. In an opioid-dependent patient, start at the low end to restore breathing without precipitating violent withdrawal.

Opioid withdrawal is **miserable but not lethal** in adults: yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, gooseflesh, dilated pupils, cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle aches. It is scored with **COWS** (`11` items; `5-12` mild, `13-24` moderate, `25-36` moderately severe, `37` or more severe). Medication for opioid use disorder: **buprenorphine** (partial agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression; must wait for moderate withdrawal, generally COWS `8-12` or more, or it precipitates withdrawal), **methadone** (full agonist, clinic-dispensed, QT prolongation risk), and **naltrexone** (antagonist, requires `7-10` days opioid-free first).

## Everything else

- **Stimulants** (cocaine, methamphetamine) — dilated pupils, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, paranoia, chest pain, seizure. Treat agitation with benzodiazepines and cool the patient. Cocaine chest pain gets benzodiazepines, aspirin, nitrates; avoid beta blocker monotherapy by convention.
- **Cannabis** — conjunctival injection, increased appetite, tachycardia, time distortion. **Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome** is cyclic vomiting in a heavy chronic user, classically relieved by hot showers; the treatment that matters is stopping use, with topical capsaicin and antiemetics as bridges.
- **Benzodiazepines** — withdrawal is the dangerous one: seizures and delirium, like alcohol. Taper, never stop abruptly. Flumazenil is rarely used because it can precipitate seizures.
- **Hallucinogens** — LSD and psilocybin cause vivid perceptual change with preserved insight; treat with a quiet room and reassurance. PCP is different: nystagmus, violence, analgesia, and true danger.
- **Tobacco** — the highest-yield conversation in medicine. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, and bupropion roughly double to triple quit rates, and combining counseling with medication beats either alone.

> **Trap:** Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill. Opioid withdrawal generally does not. Students reverse this constantly.
keyPoints: Substance use disorder severity: 2-3 mild, 4-5 moderate, 6 or more of 11 criteria severe.
Alcohol withdrawal clock: tremor 6-12 h, hallucinosis 12-24 h, seizures 24-48 h, delirium tremens 48-72 h and beyond.
Benzodiazepines treat alcohol withdrawal, dosed by CIWA-Ar; thiamine goes in before glucose.
Opioid overdose triad is depressed consciousness, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils; naloxone 0.4-2 mg, repeat every 2-3 minutes.
Buprenorphine needs moderate withdrawal (COWS roughly 8-12) before the first dose or it precipitates withdrawal.

checks.q: A patient's last drink was 60 hours ago. He is now febrile to 38.6 C, tachycardic at 128, drenched in sweat, and disoriented. This is:
checks.why: Delirium tremens appears 48-72 hours out with confusion plus autonomic instability. Alcoholic hallucinosis occurs at 12-24 hours with intact orientation, and Wernicke is confusion, ataxia, and eye findings without an autonomic storm.

checks.q: Why must thiamine be given before or with glucose in a malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder?
choices: Glucose inactivates thiamine in the stomach
Thiamine raises the seizure threshold only when glucose is low
A glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine deficiency
Thiamine is required for naloxone to work
checks.why: Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism. Loading glucose into a depleted patient consumes remaining thiamine and can trigger Wernicke encephalopathy.

checks.q: A patient with opioid use disorder is given buprenorphine while still comfortable, only 4 hours after his last dose of a full agonist. The expected result is:
checks.why: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist. Given before moderate withdrawal it displaces the full agonist and abruptly lowers receptor activity, precipitating severe withdrawal.

lessons.title: Psychiatric medications and their emergencies
lessons.body:
You do not need to prescribe yet. You do need to know what these drugs do, how long they take, and which combinations turn into an emergency.

## Antidepressants

**SSRIs** (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine) and **SNRIs** (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are first-line. Mechanism: block reuptake, raising synaptic serotonin (and norepinephrine for SNRIs). Onset is the number people forget — some effect in `1-2` weeks, full response at **4-6 weeks**. Side effects: nausea and headache early, sexual dysfunction and weight change later, hyponatremia in older adults, and a small bleeding risk.

**Discontinuation syndrome** follows abrupt stopping of short half-life agents, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine: dizziness, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, electric-shock sensations. Fluoxetine's long half-life largely protects against it. Taper.

There is a **black box warning** for increased suicidal thinking and behavior in patients under age `25`. Energy often returns before mood does, so follow up early — typically within `1-2` weeks of starting.

Other agents worth knowing: **bupropion** (norepinephrine-dopamine, no sexual side effects, helps smoking cessation; lowers the seizure threshold, so avoid in eating disorders and seizure disorder), **mirtazapine** (sedating, increases appetite — useful in the underweight insomniac), **trazodone** (used mostly for sleep; priapism is the rare, real risk). **TCAs** (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) are effective but lethal in overdose through QRS widening and arrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote. **MAOIs** require a tyramine-restricted diet — aged cheese, cured meats, draft beer — or a hypertensive crisis follows, and they must never be combined with serotonergic drugs.

## Two syndromes, side by side

| | Serotonin syndrome | Neuroleptic malignant syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Serotonergic drugs, often a new one added | Dopamine blockers, or abrupt dopamine agonist withdrawal |
| Onset | Hours | Days to weeks |
| Neuromuscular | **Hyperreflexia, clonus**, especially lower limbs | **Lead-pipe rigidity**, hyporeflexia |
| Pupils | Dilated | Normal |
| Bowel sounds | Hyperactive | Normal or decreased |
| Labs | Variable | Very high creatine kinase, high white count |
| Treatment | Stop the drug, cool, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine | Stop the drug, cool, dantrolene, bromocriptine |

> **Key:** Clonus and hyperreflexia mean serotonin syndrome. Lead-pipe rigidity with a sky-high creatine kinase means neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

## Antipsychotics

**First-generation** (haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine) block D2 strongly and cause more movement side effects. **Second-generation** (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone) add serotonin blockade, cause fewer movement effects, and bring metabolic burden — weight gain, dyslipidemia, diabetes. Olanzapine is the metabolic worst offender; ziprasidone and aripiprazole are lighter.

**Extrapyramidal symptoms** follow a timeline:

1. **Acute dystonia** — hours to days. Sustained muscle contraction, torticollis, oculogyric crisis. Treat with diphenhydramine `25-50` mg or benztropine `1-2` mg.
2. **Akathisia** — days to weeks. Unbearable inner restlessness, cannot sit still. Frequently misread as worsening agitation, which leads to more antipsychotic and a worse patient. Reduce the dose; propranolol helps.
3. **Parkinsonism** — weeks to months. Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia.
4. **Tardive dyskinesia** — months to years. Involuntary choreoathetoid movements, classically lip-smacking and tongue movements. Often irreversible; VMAT2 inhibitors are the treatment.

**Clozapine** is the most effective agent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and the only one with an anti-suicidal indication, but it causes **agranulocytosis** in roughly `1%`, requiring absolute neutrophil count monitoring — weekly for `6` months, then every `2` weeks, then monthly. It also carries myocarditis, seizure, and severe constipation risk.

## Mood stabilizers and the rest

**Lithium**: therapeutic level `0.6-1.2` mEq/L, and the toxic threshold sits just above it. Toxicity brings tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, ataxia, confusion, seizure; hemodialysis is the definitive treatment in severe cases. Monitor level, renal function, and thyroid function. Dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides, and ACE inhibitors all raise the level.

**Valproate**: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, and it is a major teratogen (neural tube defects). **Lamotrigine**: titrate slowly because of **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**; it is the better choice for the depressed pole of bipolar disorder. **Benzodiazepines**: fast, effective, and habit-forming — short courses. **Stimulants** for ADHD: effective within an hour, watch appetite, sleep, blood pressure, and diversion.

> **Trap:** A patient on an antipsychotic who "cannot sit still" is usually experiencing akathisia, not escalating psychosis. More antipsychotic makes it worse.
keyPoints: SSRIs take 4-6 weeks for full effect; taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome.
Black box warning for suicidality under age 25 — follow up within 1-2 weeks of starting.
Serotonin syndrome: hours, clonus, hyperreflexia. NMS: days, lead-pipe rigidity, very high creatine kinase.
EPS timeline: dystonia hours, akathisia days to weeks, parkinsonism weeks to months, tardive dyskinesia months to years.
Lithium therapeutic range is 0.6-1.2 mEq/L; clozapine requires scheduled neutrophil monitoring.

checks.q: Six hours after tramadol is added to a patient's sertraline, he becomes agitated, diaphoretic, and febrile with lower-limb clonus and dilated pupils. The diagnosis is:
checks.why: Rapid onset after adding a serotonergic drug, with clonus, hyperreflexia, and dilated pupils, is serotonin syndrome. NMS develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia.

checks.q: A patient started on haloperidol 3 days ago reports an unbearable need to keep moving and paces constantly. The correct interpretation is:
choices: Worsening psychosis requiring a higher dose
checks.why: Akathisia appears within days to weeks as inner restlessness. Raising the antipsychotic dose worsens it. Dystonia is sustained contraction; tardive dyskinesia takes months to years.

checks.q: Which lithium level is within the standard therapeutic range?
checks.why: The therapeutic range is 0.6-1.2 mEq/L. 0.2 is subtherapeutic; 1.8 and 2.5 are in the toxic range where tremor, ataxia, confusion, and seizures occur.

lessons.title: Consent, commitment, and special populations
lessons.body:
Psychiatry is the specialty where the law walks into the room with the patient. These rules are testable and, more importantly, they protect people.

## Capacity versus competency

**Competency** is a legal status decided by a judge, and it is global. **Capacity** is a clinical judgment made by a clinician about *one specific decision at one moment*. A person can have capacity to consent to a chest radiograph and lack it for a lung resection.

The four-part capacity test asks whether the person can:

1. **Communicate** a stable choice
2. **Understand** the relevant information
3. **Appreciate** how it applies to their own situation
4. **Reason** — compare options and their consequences

> **Trap:** Refusing the recommended treatment is not evidence of incapacity. A person with capacity is allowed to make a decision you think is wrong. Psychiatric diagnosis alone does not remove capacity either.

**Informed consent** requires disclosure of the diagnosis, the treatment, its risks and benefits, the alternatives, and the consequences of doing nothing — plus voluntariness and capacity. Exceptions: a true emergency, and a patient who waives the discussion.

## Commitment

**Involuntary** commitment generally requires mental illness *plus* danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability — an inability to meet basic needs. It authorizes *detention and evaluation*, not automatic forced medication; involuntary treatment is a separate legal question except in an emergency.

In **New Jersey**, at recognition level: a state-certified screening service performs the screening, and a **Screening Certificate** completed by a qualified screener plus a physician can hold a person for emergency evaluation, followed by court review. The principle to carry, whatever the state: commitment is time-limited, reviewable, and requires the least restrictive setting that is safe.

## Confidentiality and its limits

Protected by HIPAA and, for federally assisted substance use treatment records, by the stricter **42 CFR Part 2**. Limits: imminent danger to self or others, suspected child or elder abuse (mandatory reporting), certain communicable diseases, and court orders.

**Duty to warn** comes from *Tarasoff*: when a patient makes a credible threat against an identifiable victim, the clinician may have a duty to protect, which can include warning the victim and notifying police. The exact rule varies by state.

**Minors** generally need parental consent, with state-varying exceptions: emancipated minors, and care for sexually transmitted infections, contraception, pregnancy, and substance use treatment. Emergency care never waits for consent.

## Psychotherapies, at recognition

- **Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)** — identify and restructure distorted thoughts; first-line for depression, anxiety, and insomnia.
- **Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)** — mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness; the evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder.
- **Exposure and response prevention** — graded contact with the feared stimulus without the compulsion; the treatment for OCD and phobias.
- **Motivational interviewing** — draw out the person's own reasons to change; substance use.
- **Psychodynamic therapy** — unconscious patterns and past relationships.
- **Group and family therapy** — shared experience, systems change.

## Perinatal, pediatric, geriatric, and ECT

**Baby blues** affects up to `80%` of new mothers, starts within days, peaks around day `5`, and resolves by **2 weeks**. It needs support, not medication. **Postpartum depression** meets full depressive criteria, begins in pregnancy or within weeks to months of delivery, affects roughly `10%` to `15%`, and is treated. **Postpartum psychosis** is a **psychiatric emergency** — roughly `1` to `2` per `1000` births, onset usually in the first `2` weeks, with confusion, delusions, and risk to mother and infant. It means hospitalization, not a follow-up appointment.

Children present differently: depression often looks like irritability, anxiety like somatic complaints or school refusal. Older adults have higher suicide completion rates, present depression as cognitive complaint (pseudodementia), and are sensitive to anticholinergic and sedating drugs — start low, go slow.

**Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)** is the most effective treatment for severe depression, used for treatment resistance, catatonia, psychotic depression, severe suicidality, and pregnancy where medication is undesirable. Response rates reach `70%` to `90%`. The main side effect is memory disturbance around the treatment period. Raised intracranial pressure is the classic relative contraindication.

> **On the exam:** New mother, day `4`, tearful and overwhelmed but bonding and safe — baby blues, reassess in two weeks. New mother, day `10`, confused with delusions about the baby — postpartum psychosis, admit now.
keyPoints: Capacity is clinical, decision-specific, and tested on communicate, understand, appreciate, reason; competency is a judge's global ruling.
Refusing treatment is not proof of incapacity, and a psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity.
Involuntary commitment needs mental illness plus danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability.
Duty to warn arises with a credible threat to an identifiable victim; the exact obligation varies by state.
Baby blues resolves by 2 weeks; postpartum psychosis is an emergency admission.

checks.q: A patient with schizophrenia declines a recommended appendectomy but can explain the diagnosis, the risks of refusing, and why he is choosing to wait. Regarding capacity:
choices: He lacks capacity because he has schizophrenia
He lacks capacity because he refused the recommendation
He has capacity for this decision
Only a judge can make this determination
checks.why: He communicates a choice, understands, appreciates, and reasons. Neither a psychiatric diagnosis nor refusal of the recommended option removes capacity; competency is the judge's global ruling, not this decision.

checks.q: A woman 9 days postpartum is brought in confused, with delusions that her infant is possessed. The correct action is:
choices: Reassure that this is baby blues and recheck in 2 weeks
Start an SSRI and arrange outpatient follow-up
checks.why: Confusion plus delusions in the early postpartum period is postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with real risk to mother and infant. Baby blues has no psychosis and resolves by 2 weeks.

cards.front: What is the difference between history and the mental status exam?
cards.back: History is what the patient reports about the past. The MSE is what you observe in the room right now. Keep them in separate sections of the note.

cards.front: How do you document mood versus affect?
cards.back: Mood is the patient's own words in quotation marks. Affect is your observation, described by quality, range (full, constricted, flat), and congruence with the stated mood.

cards.front: What is the difference between thought process and thought content?
cards.back: Process is the form of thinking: linear, circumstantial, tangential, flight of ideas, loose associations. Content is the subject matter: delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal ideation.

cards.front: Circumstantial versus tangential thinking — what separates them?
cards.back: Circumstantial speech wanders through detours but eventually arrives at the point. Tangential speech wanders and never gets there.

cards.front: What are the cutoff scores for the MMSE and MoCA?
cards.back: MMSE is scored out of 30; below 24 suggests impairment. MoCA is also out of 30, with 26 or higher considered normal. Both are screens, not diagnoses.

cards.front: Which hallucination type points away from primary psychiatric illness?
cards.back: New visual or tactile hallucinations. Auditory hallucinations are the most common type in primary psychiatric illness; visual and tactile suggest delirium, intoxication, or withdrawal.

cards.front: How many criteria and how long for major depressive disorder?
cards.back: Five of nine symptoms nearly every day for at least 2 weeks, and at least one must be depressed mood or anhedonia, with distress or impairment.

cards.front: What does SIGECAPS stand for?
cards.back: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor change, Suicidality — the eight symptoms besides depressed mood in major depression.

cards.front: What are the PHQ-9 severity bands?
cards.back: 0-4 minimal, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, 20-27 severe. Item 9 asks about thoughts of death and any positive answer triggers risk assessment.

cards.front: How long must a persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) last?
cards.back: Depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years in adults, or 1 year in children and adolescents.

cards.front: What duration separates mania from hypomania?
cards.back: Mania lasts at least 7 days, or any duration if hospitalization is needed. Hypomania lasts at least 4 consecutive days with no marked impairment and no psychosis.

cards.front: What distinguishes bipolar I from bipolar II?
cards.back: Bipolar I requires at least one lifetime manic episode. Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode, and never a manic episode.

cards.front: Why is antidepressant monotherapy risky in bipolar disorder?
cards.back: It can flip the patient into mania or accelerate cycling. Screen every depressed patient for past manic or hypomanic episodes before starting an antidepressant.

cards.front: How long must generalized anxiety disorder symptoms last, and how many associated features?
cards.back: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple domains, more days than not, for at least 6 months, with 3 or more of 6 associated symptoms (1 in children).

cards.front: Define a panic attack and what turns it into panic disorder.
cards.back: A panic attack is a discrete fear surge peaking within 10 minutes with 4 or more of 13 symptoms. Panic disorder adds recurrent unexpected attacks plus 1 month of worry or avoidance.

cards.front: What are the GAD-7 cutoff scores?
cards.back: Scored 0-21: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 severe. A score of 10 or higher is the usual threshold for referral or treatment.

cards.front: Name the four PTSD symptom clusters.
cards.back: Intrusion, avoidance, negative changes in cognition and mood, and altered arousal and reactivity — all following a qualifying trauma exposure.

cards.front: What duration separates acute stress disorder from PTSD?
cards.back: Acute stress disorder lasts 3 days to 1 month after the trauma. PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month.

cards.front: How do obsessions and compulsions differ in function?
cards.back: Obsessions are intrusive unwanted thoughts that raise anxiety. Compulsions are repetitive acts done to lower it, which works briefly and reinforces the obsession long-term.

cards.front: Why does a first panic-like episode after age 45 demand a workup?
cards.back: Because arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycemia, and pheochromocytoma all mimic panic. Panic disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion at that age.

cards.front: What are positive versus negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
cards.back: Positive symptoms are added: hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behavior. Negative symptoms are subtracted: flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal.

cards.front: Which symptom group drives long-term disability in schizophrenia?
cards.back: Negative and cognitive symptoms. Positive symptoms respond to antipsychotics; negative symptoms respond poorly and determine functional outcome.

cards.front: Give the duration thresholds for the psychotic disorders.
cards.back: Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to under 1 month. Schizophreniform: 1 to 6 months. Schizophrenia: 6 months or more, including at least 1 month of active symptoms.

cards.front: What defines schizoaffective disorder?
cards.back: A mood episode plus psychosis, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations with no prominent mood episode. That 2-week window separates it from mood disorder with psychotic features.

cards.front: What defines delusional disorder?
cards.back: At least 1 month of delusions with otherwise preserved functioning and no other active-phase schizophrenia symptoms. Behavior outside the delusion often looks normal.

cards.front: What belongs in a first-episode psychosis workup?
cards.back: Vitals with temperature, fingerstick glucose, CBC, metabolic panel, TSH, urine drug screen, urinalysis, pregnancy test where applicable, and imaging when atypical or after age 40.

cards.front: What is the typical age of onset for schizophrenia?
cards.back: Late teens to mid-20s in men, late 20s to early 30s in women. Lifetime prevalence is about 0.3% to 0.7%, and roughly 5% die by suicide.

cards.front: Name the three personality disorder clusters and their themes.
cards.back: Cluster A odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal). Cluster B dramatic or erratic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic). Cluster C anxious or fearful (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive).

cards.front: How do you tell schizoid from avoidant personality disorder?
cards.back: Schizoid genuinely does not want relationships. Avoidant wants them badly but avoids people out of fear of rejection and humiliation.

cards.front: What age requirements define antisocial personality disorder?
cards.back: The patient must be at least 18 years old, with evidence of conduct disorder beginning before age 15, plus a pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights.

cards.front: What medical findings signal danger in anorexia nervosa?
cards.back: Bradycardia below 40, hypotension, hypothermia, QT prolongation, low potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, amenorrhea, osteopenia, and lanugo hair.

cards.front: What is refeeding syndrome and which electrolyte falls first?
cards.back: Carbohydrate reintroduction raises insulin, driving electrolytes intracellularly. Phosphate falls first and hardest, causing heart failure, rhabdomyolysis, and seizures. Potassium and magnesium also fall.

cards.front: How is bulimia nervosa defined, and what physical signs appear?
cards.back: Bingeing with compensatory behavior at least weekly for 3 months, usually at normal weight. Signs: dental erosion, parotid swelling, Russell sign knuckle calluses, hypokalemic alkalosis.

cards.front: What are the ADHD onset and setting requirements?
cards.back: Six or more symptoms (5 if age 17 or older) for at least 6 months, with several symptoms present before age 12, in two or more settings, causing impairment.

cards.front: What distinguishes ARFID from anorexia nervosa?
cards.back: ARFID is restriction driven by sensory aversion, lack of interest in eating, or fear of choking, with no body-image disturbance and no fear of weight gain.

cards.front: What three features define delirium?
cards.back: Acute onset over hours to days, a fluctuating course, and impaired attention — all caused by an underlying medical condition, substance, or medication.

cards.front: How do delirium and dementia differ in onset, attention, and reversibility?
cards.back: Delirium: hours to days, fluctuating, attention impaired, often reversible. Dementia: months to years, slowly progressive, attention preserved until late, rarely reversible.

cards.front: Which delirium subtype is most often missed, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Hypoactive delirium — quiet and withdrawn, mistaken for depression. It is the most common subtype and carries the worst outcomes because the cause goes unfound.

cards.front: What does the DIMS frame cover in a delirium workup?
cards.back: Drugs, Infection, Metabolic, Structural. Practically: vitals, glucose, medication review, CBC, electrolytes with calcium, renal and liver function, urinalysis, chest radiograph, ECG.

cards.front: Which dementia features visual hallucinations plus antipsychotic sensitivity?
cards.back: Lewy body dementia: fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics such as haloperidol.

cards.front: Which dementia changes personality before memory?
cards.back: Frontotemporal dementia, typically onset age 45 to 65, with disinhibition, apathy, and loss of empathy preceding memory loss. It is often mistaken for primary psychiatric illness.

cards.front: Name six medical conditions that can masquerade as psychiatric illness.
cards.back: Thyroid disease, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, infection, vitamin B12 deficiency, and neurosyphilis. Also Wilson disease, Huntington disease, brain lesions, steroids, and anticholinergics.

cards.front: Does asking about suicide increase risk?
cards.back: No. Asking directly does not plant the idea; the evidence is consistent. Not asking is the error. Ask plainly and then assess plan, intent, means, and prior attempts.

cards.front: What is the strongest single predictor of a future suicide attempt?
cards.back: A prior suicide attempt. Other strong static factors include male sex for completion, age over 65 or adolescence, substance use, chronic illness, and firearm access.

cards.front: Why is means restriction so effective?
cards.back: Most suicidal crises are brief. Removing firearms and limiting medication quantity during that window prevents the act from being available at the moment of highest risk.

cards.front: What belongs in a safety plan?
cards.back: Warning signs, internal coping steps, distracting people and places, people to ask for help, professionals and crisis lines including 988, and means restriction. Written with the patient, not handed over.

cards.front: What does room safety for a high-risk patient involve?
cards.back: Gown the patient, search and remove belongings, sharps, cords, belts, shoelaces, lighters, and medications, strip equipment and tubing, use a line-of-sight room, and assign continuous observation.

cards.front: List the agitation management ladder in order.
cards.back: Verbal de-escalation first, then environmental measures, then chemical medication offered orally before intramuscular, then physical restraint only for imminent danger.

cards.front: What are the maximum restraint order durations by age?
cards.back: 4 hours for adults 18 and older, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour for children under 9, with re-evaluation required to renew. Never restrain prone.

cards.front: How is substance use disorder severity graded in DSM-5?
cards.back: By how many of 11 criteria are met: 2-3 mild, 4-5 moderate, 6 or more severe. Tolerance and withdrawal on an appropriately prescribed medication do not count toward a disorder.

cards.front: What is the alcohol withdrawal timeline?
cards.back: 6-12 hours tremor and autonomic symptoms; 12-24 hours alcoholic hallucinosis with intact orientation; 24-48 hours withdrawal seizures; 48-72 hours and beyond delirium tremens.

cards.front: How is alcohol withdrawal treated, and what tool guides dosing?
cards.back: Benzodiazepines dosed to symptoms using CIWA-Ar, treating at roughly 8-10 or higher. Lorazepam is preferred in liver disease. Add thiamine, folate, magnesium, and fluids.

cards.front: Why give thiamine before glucose, and what does deficiency cause?
cards.back: Glucose consumes remaining thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus. Chronically it becomes Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation.

cards.front: What is the opioid overdose triad and the naloxone dose?
cards.back: Depressed consciousness, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils. Naloxone 0.4 to 2 mg IV, IM, or IN (4 mg intranasal device), repeated every 2-3 minutes; expect re-sedation.

cards.front: Which withdrawal syndromes can kill, and which usually cannot?
cards.back: Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill through seizures and delirium. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely lethal in otherwise healthy adults.

cards.front: Why must buprenorphine wait for moderate withdrawal?
cards.back: It is a high-affinity partial agonist. Given too early it displaces the full agonist and drops receptor activity abruptly, precipitating withdrawal. Wait for COWS around 8-12 or higher.

cards.front: What is cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome?
cards.back: Cyclic vomiting and abdominal pain in a heavy chronic cannabis user, classically relieved by hot showers. The definitive treatment is stopping use; capsaicin cream and antiemetics bridge.

cards.front: How long do SSRIs take to work, and what is the black box warning?
cards.back: Some effect in 1-2 weeks, full response at 4-6 weeks. Black box warning for increased suicidal thinking and behavior in patients under age 25; follow up within 1-2 weeks.

cards.front: What is antidepressant discontinuation syndrome?
cards.back: Dizziness, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, and electric-shock sensations after abruptly stopping a short half-life agent such as paroxetine or venlafaxine. Fluoxetine's long half-life protects. Taper.

cards.front: How do serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome differ?
cards.back: Serotonin syndrome: onset in hours, clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, hyperactive bowel sounds. NMS: onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, very high creatine kinase.

cards.front: How are serotonin syndrome and NMS treated?
cards.back: Both: stop the offending drug, cool aggressively, support. Serotonin syndrome adds benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine. NMS adds dantrolene and bromocriptine.

cards.front: What is the extrapyramidal symptom timeline?
cards.back: Acute dystonia in hours to days, akathisia in days to weeks, parkinsonism in weeks to months, tardive dyskinesia in months to years.

cards.front: How is acute dystonia treated?
cards.back: Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg or benztropine 1-2 mg, given IV or IM, with rapid relief of torticollis, oculogyric crisis, or other sustained contraction.

cards.front: Why is clozapine monitored so closely?
cards.back: It causes agranulocytosis in roughly 1%, so absolute neutrophil count is checked weekly for 6 months, then every 2 weeks, then monthly. Myocarditis, seizure, and severe constipation also occur.

cards.front: What is the lithium therapeutic range and what raises the level?
cards.back: 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. Dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, and ACE inhibitors raise it. Toxicity brings tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, ataxia, confusion, and seizures; dialysis treats severe cases.

cards.front: What are the key warnings for valproate and lamotrigine?
cards.back: Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, and major teratogenicity with neural tube defects. Lamotrigine: titrate slowly because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

cards.front: What is the four-part test of decision-making capacity?
cards.back: Can the person communicate a stable choice, understand the information, appreciate how it applies to them, and reason through the options and consequences?

cards.front: How do capacity and competency differ?
cards.back: Capacity is a clinical judgment about one specific decision at one moment, made by a clinician. Competency is a global legal status decided by a judge.

cards.front: What three grounds usually justify involuntary commitment?
cards.back: Mental illness plus danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability (inability to meet basic needs). It authorizes detention and evaluation, not automatic forced medication.

cards.front: What is the duty to warn, and where does it come from?
cards.back: From the Tarasoff cases: when a patient makes a credible threat against an identifiable victim, the clinician may have a duty to protect, which can include warning the victim and police. Rules vary by state.

cards.front: Distinguish baby blues, postpartum depression, and postpartum psychosis.
cards.back: Baby blues: up to 80%, peaks day 5, resolves by 2 weeks, no treatment. Postpartum depression: 10-15%, full criteria, treated. Postpartum psychosis: 1-2 per 1000, emergency admission.

cards.front: Which therapy is first-line for borderline personality disorder, and which for OCD?
cards.back: Dialectical behavior therapy for borderline personality disorder. Exposure and response prevention for OCD and phobias. CBT is first-line for depression, anxiety, and insomnia.

quiz.q: A patient states "I'm doing great" while sitting motionless with no facial expression and a monotone voice. How should the MSE read?
choices: Mood "I'm doing great"; affect flat and incongruent with stated mood
quiz.why: Mood is the patient's quoted self-report; affect is your observation with range and congruence. Reversing the two, or accepting the report at face value, loses the key finding: incongruence.

quiz.q: Which MSE component describes whether a patient believes they are ill?
quiz.why: Insight is awareness of one's own illness. Judgment is the safety of decisions described. Thought process is the form of thinking, and cognition covers orientation, attention, and memory.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with new confusion has a MoCA of 19 of 30. The most accurate interpretation is:
choices: The screen is abnormal and requires further evaluation
The result is normal for his age
quiz.why: MoCA 26 or higher is normal, so 19 is abnormal — but it is a screen. It cannot distinguish delirium, dementia, or depression, all of which require further evaluation and a search for medical causes.

quiz.q: A 33-year-old reports 3 weeks of anhedonia, insomnia, fatigue, poor concentration, 8-pound weight loss, and guilt. She denies suicidal ideation. Which statement is correct?
choices: She does not meet criteria because there is no suicidal ideation
She meets criteria for major depressive disorder
She meets criteria for persistent depressive disorder
She needs 6 weeks of symptoms to qualify
quiz.why: Five or more of nine symptoms for at least 2 weeks with anhedonia present meets major depressive disorder. Suicidal ideation is one optional criterion, not a requirement. Persistent depressive disorder requires 2 years.

quiz.q: Which symptom best distinguishes a manic episode from major depression with insomnia?
choices: Decreased need for sleep with preserved energy
quiz.why: In mania the patient sleeps little and feels rested and energized. In depression with insomnia the patient sleeps little and feels exhausted. Decreased need, not decreased amount, is the discriminator.

quiz.q: A 28-year-old with a history of one hypomanic episode and two major depressive episodes has which diagnosis?
choices: Major depressive disorder with mixed features
quiz.why: Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode and no manic episode. Bipolar I requires a full manic episode; cyclothymia requires 2 years of subthreshold symptoms.

quiz.q: A depressed patient is about to be started on an antidepressant. Which history is most important to obtain first?
quiz.why: Antidepressant monotherapy in undiagnosed bipolar disorder can precipitate mania or rapid cycling. Screening for past mania before prescribing is the standard step; the other items do not change the decision.

quiz.q: A patient worries excessively about work, money, and health on most days for the past 8 months, with muscle tension, irritability, and poor sleep. Most likely:
quiz.why: Multi-domain excessive worry for 6 months or more with 3 or more associated symptoms is GAD. Panic disorder centers on discrete attacks, social anxiety on scrutiny, and adjustment disorder on an identifiable stressor within 3 months.

quiz.q: A soldier has nightmares, avoids reminders, feels detached, and startles easily 4 months after a deployment attack. The diagnosis is:
quiz.why: A qualifying trauma plus all four symptom clusters lasting more than 1 month is PTSD. Acute stress disorder is capped at 1 month, and adjustment disorder requires a non-traumatic stressor.

quiz.q: A patient washes her hands 40 times daily, knows it is excessive, and does it to reduce anxiety about contamination. The compulsion's role is best described as:
choices: Temporarily lowering anxiety while reinforcing the obsession
quiz.why: Compulsions relieve anxiety for minutes and strengthen the obsessive loop over time. The obsession causes the anxiety; the compulsion is the maladaptive relief. Insight is intact, so this is not a delusion.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old has a panic attack in a store, then spends 6 weeks fearing another and avoiding stores. This best fits:
