quiz.why: Recurrent unexpected attacks plus 1 month or more of worry about further attacks or avoidance behavior is panic disorder. Specific phobia is a fear of a defined object or situation without unexpected attacks.

quiz.q: Which symptom of schizophrenia responds least well to antipsychotic medication?
quiz.why: Negative symptoms such as avolition and flat affect respond poorly and drive long-term disability. Hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech are positive symptoms tied to mesolimbic dopamine excess and respond better.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with no psychiatric history develops paranoid delusions and visual hallucinations over 2 days. The best next step is:
choices: Start risperidone and refer to outpatient psychiatry
Begin a medical workup for delirium
quiz.why: New psychosis over 2 days in an older adult with visual hallucinations is delirium until proven otherwise. Schizophrenia rarely begins at 68, and medicating before finding the cause can worsen the outcome.

quiz.q: A patient has had psychotic symptoms for 8 months alongside recurrent depressive episodes, including a 3-week stretch of hallucinations with no mood symptoms. Most consistent with:
choices: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
quiz.why: Two or more weeks of psychosis without a prominent mood episode, in someone who also has mood episodes, defines schizoaffective disorder. In depression with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during mood episodes.

quiz.q: Which factor predicts a better prognosis in schizophrenia?
choices: Acute onset with a clear precipitant
quiz.why: Acute onset, an identifiable precipitant, prominent mood symptoms, good premorbid function, and short untreated duration predict better outcomes. Insidious early onset, negative symptoms, and poor premorbid function predict worse ones.

quiz.q: A 17-year-old with anorexia nervosa has a heart rate of 38 and a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. The most appropriate disposition is:
choices: Medical admission for monitoring and electrolyte correction
Discharge with a follow-up in 2 weeks
quiz.why: Bradycardia below 40 and hypokalemia are admission criteria in anorexia because of arrhythmia risk. Outpatient management cannot correct these safely or monitor for refeeding syndrome.

quiz.q: Which cluster B personality disorder is most associated with self-harm, chronic emptiness, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment?
quiz.why: Borderline personality disorder features unstable relationships, identity, and affect with self-harm and abandonment fears. Histrionic centers on attention-seeking, narcissistic on grandiosity, antisocial on rights violations.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old is inattentive and hyperactive at school, but his parents report no problems at home. Regarding ADHD:
choices: Criteria are met because symptoms are severe at school
Criteria are not met because impairment must appear in two or more settings
Criteria are met only if symptoms began before age 7
The diagnosis requires a positive stimulant trial
quiz.why: ADHD requires symptoms in two or more settings, for 6 months, with several present before age 12. Single-setting symptoms suggest a learning, environmental, or classroom-specific problem instead.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old is quiet, withdrawn, and minimally responsive 2 days after hip surgery. Attention testing is impaired. The most likely diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Acute onset with impaired attention after surgery is hypoactive delirium, the most common and most missed subtype. Depression and dementia do not produce acute inattention over 2 days.

quiz.q: Which single test is most essential in any patient with acute behavioral change?
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible and lethal if missed, and it produces confusion, agitation, and bizarre behavior. The other tests are useful but not the immediate bedside priority.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old develops disinhibition, socially inappropriate remarks, and apathy over a year, with memory relatively preserved. Most likely:
quiz.why: Personality and behavioral change preceding memory loss, with onset typically age 45-65, is frontotemporal dementia. Alzheimer begins with short-term memory loss; vascular is stepwise; Lewy body brings visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.

quiz.q: A patient has a slowly progressive dementia, paresthesias in the feet, and a macrocytic anemia. The mimic to evaluate is:
quiz.why: B12 deficiency produces cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, and posterior column paresthesias with macrocytosis. Normal pressure hydrocephalus gives gait, urinary, and cognitive changes without anemia.

quiz.q: Which statement about asking patients directly about suicide is correct?
choices: Asking directly does not increase risk and is the standard of care
Asking can plant the idea and should be avoided
Only psychiatrists may ask about suicide
Asking is only appropriate when the PHQ-9 is above 15
quiz.why: Evidence consistently shows direct questioning does not increase risk. Avoiding the question is the error, and any clinician can and should ask when concern exists, regardless of a score.

quiz.q: Which intervention most reduces near-term suicide risk in a patient discharged home?
choices: Removing firearms from the home and limiting medication quantity
quiz.why: Means restriction targets the brief window of highest risk and has the strongest evidence. Delayed referral and passive advice do nothing during the crisis itself.

quiz.q: An agitated intoxicated patient has failed verbal de-escalation and is now swinging at staff. Physical restraints are placed. Which action is required?
choices: Place him prone to limit movement
Leave restraints on until the morning shift
Obtain a time-limited order and monitor on a set schedule
Restrain without an order since it is an emergency
quiz.why: Restraint requires a provider order with age-based time limits (4 hours for adults) and scheduled monitoring of circulation, airway, and skin. Prone positioning risks positional asphyxia and open-ended restraint is prohibited.

quiz.q: Which is the best predictor of future violence in a patient?
quiz.why: Past violence is the strongest predictor. Diagnosis alone is a weak predictor and most people with schizophrenia are never violent; demographics and housing status are far weaker signals.

quiz.q: A man whose last drink was 30 hours ago has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which stage of alcohol withdrawal is this?
quiz.why: Withdrawal seizures cluster at 24-48 hours. Hallucinosis is 12-24 hours with intact orientation, and delirium tremens begins at 48-72 hours with autonomic instability and confusion.

quiz.q: A patient in alcohol withdrawal with cirrhosis needs a benzodiazepine. Which is generally preferred?
quiz.why: Lorazepam is conjugated rather than oxidatively metabolized, so it does not accumulate in liver disease. Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam are long-acting and rely on hepatic oxidation.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has a respiratory rate of 5 and pinpoint pupils. After supporting ventilation, the next step is:
quiz.why: The opioid triad calls for naloxone, repeated every 2-3 minutes with observation for re-sedation. Flumazenil targets benzodiazepines and can precipitate seizures; charcoal is useless in an unprotected airway.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old heavy cannabis user has months of cyclic vomiting relieved only by long hot showers. The definitive treatment is:
quiz.why: Cannabinoid hyperemesis resolves only with cessation. Antiemetics including ondansetron work poorly, and acid suppression or surgery treats the wrong problem entirely.

quiz.q: A patient started on sertraline 10 days ago calls saying he feels no better. The best response is:
choices: Full response typically takes 4 to 6 weeks; continue and follow up
Stop sertraline immediately and switch drugs
quiz.why: SSRIs show partial effect in 1-2 weeks and full response at 4-6 weeks. Stopping early causes discontinuation symptoms, and combining two SSRIs raises serotonin syndrome risk without benefit.

quiz.q: A patient on haloperidol for 9 days becomes rigid with a temperature of 40 C, a creatine kinase of 12,000, and hyporeflexia. The treatment includes:
quiz.why: Days of onset with lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, and very high creatine kinase is neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop the antipsychotic and give dantrolene with bromocriptine. Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome.

quiz.q: A patient on lithium develops vomiting, diarrhea, coarse tremor, and ataxia after starting a thiazide diuretic. The mechanism is:
choices: The thiazide displaces lithium from plasma proteins
The thiazide increases lithium reabsorption and raises the level
quiz.why: Thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and dehydration all raise lithium levels, and the therapeutic range of 0.6-1.2 mEq/L sits right beneath toxicity. Lithium is not protein-bound to a meaningful degree.

quiz.q: A patient on an antipsychotic for 3 years develops involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements. This is:
quiz.why: Tardive dyskinesia appears after months to years as choreoathetoid oral and facial movements and is often irreversible. Dystonia occurs in hours, akathisia in days to weeks, parkinsonism in weeks to months.

quiz.q: A patient with advanced cancer refuses chemotherapy, explains the prognosis accurately, states why he prefers comfort care, and holds to that choice over two visits. Regarding capacity:
choices: He has capacity for this decision
He lacks capacity because the decision shortens his life
A psychiatric consult is required to grant capacity
A judge must rule before the refusal is honored
quiz.why: He communicates, understands, appreciates, and reasons, which satisfies the four-part test. A choice you disagree with is not incapacity, and capacity is a clinical judgment, not a court ruling.

quiz.q: A patient tells you he intends to kill a named coworker and describes how. The most appropriate action is:
choices: Document the threat and take no further step
Assess the threat and take protective action, which may include warning the person and police
Discharge him with an outpatient referral
quiz.why: A credible threat against an identifiable victim triggers the Tarasoff duty to protect, which may include warning and notification; specifics vary by state. Confidentiality yields to imminent danger.

quiz.q: A woman 5 days postpartum is tearful and overwhelmed but sleeping when the baby sleeps, bonding well, and denies any thoughts of harm. The best next step is:
choices: Reassurance, support, and reassessment in 2 weeks
quiz.why: This is baby blues: peaks around day 5 and resolves by 2 weeks without medication. Admission and antipsychotics are reserved for postpartum psychosis, which involves confusion, delusions, and risk to the infant.

scenarios.title: Emergency department: 46-year-old brought in agitated and confused
scenarios.intro:
It is 2 a.m. Police bring in a 46-year-old man found shouting at parked cars. He is sweating heavily, tremulous, and cannot tell you what day it is. A friend arrives and says he drinks "about a fifth a day" and was jailed for the last three days. He has no known psychiatric history.

You are the first clinician at the bedside.

steps.prompt: He is pacing beside the stretcher, loud but not threatening. He keeps brushing at his arms, saying "get them off me." Skin is soaked. Hands shake visibly.

choices.text: Get a fingerstick glucose, a full set of vitals, and start verbal de-escalation in a quiet room
choices.feedback: Correct. Glucose and vitals take seconds and rule in or out the fastest killers, and a low-stimulation room is the first rung of the agitation ladder.

choices.text: Call for four-point restraints immediately
choices.feedback: He is agitated but not violent. Restraint is the last rung, not the first, and it does nothing about the medical cause driving the agitation.

choices.text: Assume alcohol intoxication and place him in the hallway to sober up
choices.feedback: The tremor, diaphoresis, fever, and tachycardia are withdrawal, not intoxication. A hallway bed with no monitoring is how a withdrawal seizure gets missed.

choices.text: Order a psychiatric consult before any medical evaluation
choices.feedback: Reasonable instinct, wrong order. Acute confusion with abnormal vitals is medical until proven otherwise; psychiatry cannot clear an unevaluated delirium.

steps.prompt: Glucose is 104. He is oriented to person only. He tells you there are insects on the wall and asks you to look. His last drink was roughly 72 hours ago.

choices.text: Recognize likely delirium tremens and escalate: continuous monitoring, IV access, notify the attending
choices.feedback: Right. Confusion plus autonomic storm at 48-72 hours is delirium tremens, with mortality around 5% even treated. This is a critical-care problem.

choices.text: Call it alcoholic hallucinosis and plan observation only
choices.feedback: Hallucinosis occurs at 12-24 hours with intact orientation. He is disoriented and febrile at 72 hours, which is a different and far more dangerous condition.

choices.text: Diagnose new-onset schizophrenia given the hallucinations
choices.feedback: Visual hallucinations with disorientation and abnormal vitals point away from primary psychiatric illness, and schizophrenia rarely begins at 46.

choices.text: Start a CIWA-Ar assessment while arranging monitored placement
choices.feedback: Good — CIWA-Ar guides symptom-triggered dosing. Just make sure the escalation happens alongside it; scoring is not a substitute for a monitored bed.

steps.prompt: The attending asks what you want ready. He remains agitated and is now pulling at the IV.

choices.text: Benzodiazepines dosed to symptoms, plus thiamine, folate, magnesium, and IV fluids
choices.feedback: Correct. Benzodiazepines are the treatment for alcohol withdrawal because they cross-cover the same receptor. Thiamine and magnesium address the deficiencies that come with it.

choices.text: Haloperidol alone for the agitation
choices.feedback: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal physiology. They may be adjunctive for hallucinations but never replace the benzodiazepine.

choices.text: An IV dextrose bolus first, then the rest
choices.feedback: His glucose is 104, so he does not need it — and giving glucose before thiamine in a malnourished person can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

choices.text: Oral lorazepam and reassess in an hour
choices.feedback: Oral first is a good principle in general agitation, but a disoriented patient in delirium tremens who is pulling lines needs an IV route and close titration.

steps.prompt: Two hours later he is calmer and oriented to person and place. CIWA has dropped from 24 to 11. His friend asks whether he can go home tonight and what happens next.

choices.text: Explain that he needs admission for continued monitoring, and note that he will be offered treatment for alcohol use disorder
choices.feedback: Right on both counts. Delirium tremens requires inpatient monitoring, and the admission is the moment to connect him to naltrexone, acamprosate, or disulfiram and counseling.

choices.text: Discharge with a lorazepam prescription and a clinic number
choices.feedback: Dangerous. He is mid-course in delirium tremens and improvement on treatment is not resolution. Outpatient benzodiazepines here carry real overdose and relapse risk.

choices.text: Tell the friend nothing because of confidentiality
choices.feedback: Over-corrected. You may always receive collateral, and with the patient's permission you can share. Blanket refusal cuts off the support system he will need.

choices.text: Admit him and defer any substance use conversation to the outpatient team
choices.feedback: Admission is correct, but deferring the conversation wastes the highest-leverage moment. Brief intervention during admission measurably improves engagement.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **acute confusion plus abnormal vital signs is medical until proven otherwise**, and the alcohol withdrawal clock tells you which stage you are in. Tremor at 6-12 hours, hallucinosis at 12-24 hours with orientation intact, seizures at 24-48 hours, delirium tremens at 48-72 hours and beyond with confusion and autonomic storm.

Benzodiazepines treat the physiology; antipsychotics do not. Thiamine goes before glucose. And the sedation is never the goal by itself — the goal is finding and treating the cause while keeping the person safe enough to get there.

scenarios.title: Reasoning it through: the depressed patient who says no
scenarios.intro:
This is a reasoning walkthrough, not a resuscitation. You are working through the case of a 34-year-old woman seen in a primary care office. She scores 19 on the PHQ-9 and answers item 9 with "several days."

Your job is to decide what each finding actually obligates you to do, and what it does not.

steps.prompt: PHQ-9 is 19, which is the moderately severe band. Item 9 — thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself — is positive for "several days." What does this obligate?

choices.text: A direct, live suicide risk assessment right now
choices.feedback: Yes. Any non-zero item 9 requires asking directly about ideation, plan, intent, means, and prior attempts before the visit ends. The score alone is not the assessment.

choices.text: Start an SSRI and schedule a 6-week recheck
choices.feedback: Treatment is reasonable eventually, but the sequence is wrong. You do not prescribe past an unassessed positive item 9, and 6 weeks is too long for a first follow-up.

choices.text: Note the score and refer to psychiatry in a month
choices.feedback: A month-out referral leaves the risk unaddressed today. The assessment is yours to do in the room; the referral comes after.

choices.text: Repeat the PHQ-9 to confirm the score
choices.feedback: Harmless but useless. The instrument is a screen, not a target; re-scoring it does not tell you anything about her safety.

steps.prompt: You ask directly. She says she has passive thoughts of not wanting to wake up, no plan, no intent, no prior attempts, no firearm in the home, and a 6-year-old daughter she describes as the reason she keeps going. Before you decide on treatment, what is the one history question that changes the prescription?

choices.text: Whether she has ever had a period of days with little sleep, high energy, and uncharacteristic risk-taking
choices.feedback: Exactly. Screening for past mania or hypomania before starting an antidepressant is the step that prevents flipping an undiagnosed bipolar patient into mania.

choices.text: Her caffeine intake
choices.feedback: Worth knowing for sleep hygiene, but it does not change which class of medication is safe to start.

choices.text: Whether anyone in her family has hypertension
choices.feedback: Not relevant to the choice here. Family history of bipolar disorder would matter; family history of hypertension does not.

choices.text: Nothing — start an SSRI, since all depression is treated the same way
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Unscreened bipolar depression treated with antidepressant monotherapy can flip to mania or accelerate cycling.

steps.prompt: She denies any manic or hypomanic history, and so does her sister on the phone with the patient's permission. You start sertraline. She asks how long until she feels better and what she should watch for.

choices.text: Partial effect in 1-2 weeks, full response at 4-6 weeks; report worsening thoughts of self-harm immediately
choices.feedback: Correct on both. Setting the 4-6 week expectation prevents early abandonment, and naming the warning sign is the counterpart to the under-25 black box concern.

choices.text: Tell her she should feel better within 2 to 3 days
choices.feedback: False expectation. When day 3 brings nothing, people stop the medication and conclude treatment does not work for them.

choices.text: Tell her side effects are nothing to worry about
choices.feedback: Dismissive and inaccurate. Early nausea and headache, later sexual side effects, and hyponatremia in older adults are real and worth naming honestly.

choices.text: Explain the timeline and add that she should never stop abruptly
choices.feedback: Good — discontinuation syndrome is worth mentioning. Pair it with the safety instruction about worsening self-harm thoughts and you have the complete conversation.

steps.prompt: You are planning follow-up. She has no plan, no intent, no means, strong protective factors, and is willing to engage.

choices.text: Co-write a safety plan, confirm means restriction, and schedule follow-up within 1-2 weeks
choices.feedback: This is the standard. Early follow-up matters because energy often returns before mood does, which is the window of elevated risk.

choices.text: Schedule the next visit at 8 weeks since risk is low
choices.feedback: Too long. Low acute risk is not no risk, and the first weeks on an antidepressant are exactly when contact matters most.

choices.text: Add psychotherapy referral for CBT alongside medication
choices.feedback: Strong addition — CBT plus medication outperforms either alone for moderate to severe depression. It complements, rather than replaces, early follow-up and a safety plan.

choices.text: Hand her a printed safety plan template to fill out at home
choices.feedback: A safety plan works because it is built with the patient in the room, in their own words. Handing over a blank form skips the part that does the work.

scenarios.debrief:
Three patterns worth keeping.

First, a score is a flag, not an assessment. A PHQ-9 of 19 with a positive item 9 obligates a live conversation about ideation, plan, intent, means, and prior attempts.

Second, screen for mania before you write for an antidepressant. It costs one question and prevents a serious iatrogenic injury.

Third, the follow-up interval is part of the prescription. Full antidepressant response takes 4-6 weeks, but energy can return before mood does, so the first contact belongs at 1-2 weeks — with a safety plan written together and the means already restricted.
